Q49289775.summary: Between dark painted borders, a small standing figure, probably Christ, raises his hand above a bed, while at the left a man walks away with the bed hoisted on his back. Painted in a simple outline style for the baptistery of the Christian house-church at Dura-Europos, it is among the very oldest surviving images of Jesus. For those being baptised, the healed man carrying his bed spoke of new life and restored strength given by Christ.
facts: The Dura-Europos house church, converted from a private house in the 230s–240s, is the earliest identified Christian house church; it was buried under a Roman defensive ramp before the city fell to the Persians in 256, which preserved its paintings.
The fragment measures about 145 × 88 cm and was brought to Yale after the Yale–French excavations (credited 'Yale-French Excavations at Dura-Europos').
Only the baptistery of the house church was painted; this miracle scene belonged to a register of smaller scenes above a larger procession of women.

links.label: Yale University Art Gallery object page
Wikipedia: Healing the paralytic at Bethesda

Q49289775.notes: Yale dates the painting 'ca. A.D. 232' (the house's construction inscription is dated 232/233; conversion to a church may be c. 240/241). Whether the scene follows Mark 2 (Capernaum) or John 5 (Bethesda) is debated; Wikidata links it to Bethesda, the Wikipedia article to Mark 2.

cur:manuscripts-khludov-nikephoros-icon-.summary: The saintly Patriarch Nikephoros, in white vestments, holds up a round icon with the bust of Christ and tramples the iconoclast John the Grammarian, who lies on the ground among scattered coins; above, Saint Peter treads on Simon Magus. The image of Christ held aloft is the point of the whole page: the defence of icons as a confession of the Incarnation.
facts: Many of the Khludov miniatures are polemics against the Iconoclasts, with John the Grammarian caricatured by wild, bristling hair.
Explanatory captions are written beside the figures; here they name the patriarch Nikephoros and his defeated opponent.
cur:manuscripts-khludov-nikephoros-icon-.notes: Christ appears here as a painted icon held by the patriarch. The psalm number ΝΒ (51) is visible. Folio not recorded on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts-vivian-bible-christ-in-m.summary: At the heart of a great lozenge, Christ sits on a globe within a pink mandorla, blessing and holding a book, his gold mantle swirling; the four evangelist symbols cling to the lozenge and four prophets look out from roundels at its points, while in the corners the four evangelists sit writing at their desks. The page, placed before the Gospels, unites the Old Testament prophets, the Gospel writers and the Christ of whom they all speak.
facts: The Vivian Bible was commissioned by Count Vivian, lay abbot of Saint-Martin de Tours, in 845 and presented to Charles the Bald in 846, as shown in its presentation miniature; it has 423 leaves measuring 495 by 345 mm.
It is thought to be the third illuminated Bible made at Tours, after the Bamberg Bible and the Moutier-Grandval Bible.
cur:manuscripts-vivian-bible-christ-in-m.notes: Folio 329v is the standard citation for this Majestas; a CC BY-SA scan on Commons labels the same page 'fol. 239v', apparently a transposition.

cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-lamb.summary: The Lamb with a cross-nimbus stands at the centre of the letter grid between the lion and the ox, with the eagle above and the winged man below, each holding a labelled panel. The paler palette of the Corbie copy gives the figures a delicate, drawn quality.
facts: Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, composed this cycle of figure-poems (carmina figurata) in praise of the Cross around 810; each page is a grid of letters in which shapes pick out further verses.
This manuscript came from the abbey of Corbie and is now in the municipal library of Amiens.
cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-amiens-lamb.notes: Christ is represented symbolically as the Lamb. The number in the Commons file name is the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Below the verses 'I am counted with them that go down into the pit … free among the dead … they have laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness', Christ hangs on the cross on a green ground, with a dark figure — probably Death or a demon — at the foot of the cross.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The small dark figure at the foot of the cross is not certainly identified.

cur:objects3-kells-broken-cross.summary: Only the shaft of the Broken Cross survives, but its panels are among the clearest Gospel scenes on any Irish cross. At the foot of the east face Christ stands in the Jordan, shown as two streams springing from round sources, while figures on either side attend the Baptism; in the panel above, a row of figures has been read as the Wedding Feast at Cana, where Christ worked his first sign. Even broken, the cross speaks of the new life of baptism and of the abundance of Christ's gifts.
facts: Peter Harbison identified the panels of the east face, from the bottom, as the Baptism of Christ, the Marriage Feast at Cana and, higher up, the Healing at Bethesda and Christ with the Woman of Samaria.

The Broken Cross is one of several crosses in the monastic enclosure at Kells, the house associated with St Columba and the Book of Kells; it may once have been among the tallest of all Irish high crosses.

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with Harbison's identifications)

cur:objects3-kells-broken-cross.notes: Panel identifications follow Peter Harbison as quoted on the Commons file page; the Commons description also notes that the photographer questions the Bethesda reading, since one figure appears to hold a lyre. The cross is said to have been broken in the 17th century, possibly by Cromwellian troops, but this is not documented. Date not securely established.
